readerTitle: The meal-kit deal that looked too good: spot the red flags
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (케이터링 주방 + 밀키트 구독 앱) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 재무 경고 신호는 거짓말의 증거가 아니라 '어떤 질문을 더 해야 하는지'와 '조건을 어떻게 짜야 하는지'를 알려주는 신호다.
misconception: 매출이 빠르게 늘고 이익이 났다고 하면 거래 상대로 믿어도 된다.

sources.text: 재무제표 분석의 표준 개념 (수익 인식, 현금흐름과 이익의 차이, 매출채권 연령 분석, 조정 지표, 내부 통제)
모든 회사와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 조정 이익 계산: 'Adjusted profit' $150,000에서 매달 반복되는 출시 마케팅 $120,000와 상한 키트 환불 $60,000를 다시 빼면 150,000 − 120,000 − 60,000 = −$30,000.
매출채권: 기업 고객 미수금이 $90,000에서 $180,000로 두 배, 그중 $70,000가 120일 이상 연체라는 설정. 모두 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: The meal-kit deal that looked too good
body: You run a catering kitchen. A fast-growing meal-kit app wants you to cook 2,000 kits a week for it.
The pitch deck says revenue tripled to $1.2 million and the company is profitable. The catch: you'd buy $80,000 of new equipment, and they'd pay you 60 days after each delivery.

image.label: A catering kitchen with a phone showing a rising sales chart
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 스테인리스 케이터링 주방 작업대 위에 밀키트 상자가 쌓여 있고, 옆에 놓인 스마트폰 화면에 가파르게 오르는 매출 그래프. 그래프 끝에 작은 물음표. 실제 앱 로고나 브랜드는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Where did $1.2 million come from?
body: You ask for detail. About $500,000 came from annual plans sold in a December holiday sale. The app counted the full year as revenue right away.
What do you do with the $1.2 million figure?

options.text: Accept it. Customers paid, so the money is real
options.feedback: The cash arrived, but the meals mostly haven't. The app still owes eleven months of kits, and you'd be the one cooking them.

options.text: Ask how much was for meals already delivered
options.feedback: Only about one month of those plans was delivered. Revenue actually earned so far is closer to $740,000. Growth is real, but far smaller.

options.text: Ask for the number of active subscribers instead
options.feedback: Useful, but subscriber counts can be inflated too. It doesn't tell you how much revenue was earned.

cards.title: Profitable, but the bank balance is falling.
body: Say you chose B. Next, you notice the app reports a profit, yet its cash fell for six months. Money owed by its office-lunch clients doubled to $180,000. Some of it is over 120 days late.

options.text: Trust the profit. Late payers usually pay eventually
options.feedback: Profit counts sales when they're made, not when they're paid. If $70,000 is four months late, some of it may never arrive, and the app will pay you late too.

options.text: Ask for the cash flow statement and a list of who owes what, by age
options.feedback: Now you see the gap: sales are booked, but cash isn't coming in. That tells you how likely your own invoices are to be paid on time.

options.text: Skip the analysis and demand payment upfront
options.feedback: It protects you for now, but you still don't know if the business will last long enough to justify $80,000 of equipment.

cards.title: "Adjusted profit: $150,000"
body: Say you chose B again. The founder points to *adjusted profit*. It leaves out $120,000 of "one-time launch marketing" and $60,000 of refunds for spoiled kits.
Looking closer, the launch marketing has run every single month.

options.text: Use the adjusted number. Startups need to invest in growth
options.feedback: A cost that repeats every month isn't one-time. Neither are refunds in a food business. Leaving them out hides what the business really costs to run.

options.text: Add back the costs that keep recurring
options.feedback: $150,000 − $120,000 − $60,000 = a $30,000 loss. Not fatal, but a very different company from the one in the deck.

options.text: Ignore every adjusted number they show you
options.feedback: Safe, but you lose information. Some adjustments are fair. The skill is checking which costs are truly unusual.

cards.title: Who checks the books?
body: Say you chose B. Last question: the co-founder keeps the books alone. No outside accountant has ever reviewed them, and the founder hesitates to share bank statements.

options.text: Sign as offered. The growth is still impressive
options.feedback: You'd carry 60 days of unpaid cooking plus the equipment loan, for a company whose numbers no one has independently checked.

options.text: Offer a smaller trial: weekly payment, a deposit, and bank statements before scaling up
options.feedback: You keep the upside if the app is sound and limit your loss if it isn't. Their answer to these terms is itself information.
Zero risk, but also zero upside. Messy books are common in young companies, and the right terms can make the deal safe.

cards.title: A red flag is a question, not a verdict.
body: Nothing here proves the founders lied. Young companies often count revenue too early or skip outside reviews out of inexperience, not fraud.
The point of spotting red flags is to **ask sharper questions and set safer terms**. Accusing a partner too fast can cost you a good deal and a relationship.
cards.softwareNote: Subscription businesses meet the first flag often: annual plans bring cash in on day one, but the revenue is earned month by month as the service is delivered.

cards.title: Each flag pointed to a question worth asking.
body: Before you trust someone's numbers, check what was earned, what was collected, what was left out, and who checked it.
list: **Decision 1:** revenue that isn't real yet (counted before it's earned)
**Decision 2:** cash and profit disagree, and customers who don't pay
**Decision 3:** adjusted numbers that drop recurring costs
**Decision 4:** weak oversight, with no independent check
cards.callout: **Try it today:** take the last set of numbers a partner or supplier gave you. Ask one question from each line above.
